People often ask me what happens on the first day of a Chapter 11 case. Here's the answer. The petition is filed in the morning, usually online. At that moment, the automatic stay starts. It's like a wall around the company. Creditors can't call the debtor, they can't sue, and they can't take any assets. Even a bank with a very big claim has to stop. Of course, creditors aren't happy, but they aren't forgotten either. Their claims are listed, and they're paid later, under the plan. So if you represent a creditor, my advice is simple. Don't call the debtor. Follow the court, and read the case file every day.

Five years ago, my company was in serious trouble. We had three hotels in California, and after a very bad year, we owed more than twenty million dollars. I thought it was the end. My lawyer said, no, it's a new start. So we filed for Chapter 11. The first surprise was that the hotels weren't closed, and I kept my job. For eight months, every big decision was checked by the court. Then a reorganization plan was written. We sold one hotel, and the money was used to pay the creditors. The plan was approved by the judge in the spring. Today, two hotels are open, and the debt is half of what it was.

I work for a bank in Mumbai, and some of our clients are companies in the United States. When one of them files for bankruptcy there, my job starts. First, we're told about the case by a notice from the court. The notice has one very important date: the last day to file a claim. If the claim isn't filed by that date, the bank may receive nothing at all. So I prepare the documents, I calculate the amount, and our American lawyers file the claim for us. Then we wait for the reorganization plan. My advice is simple. Read every notice on the same day you receive it. In bankruptcy, the calendar is everything.
